name: VibeSynth
explanation: A monophonic analog-style synthesizer: three anti-aliased oscillators with per-osc octave and detune, a noise source, a four-pole resonant ladder filter with drive, independent filter and amplifier ADSR envelopes, and portamento glide. A stereo effects rack adds chorus, ping-pong delay and reverb, with live oscilloscope + spectrum displays. Play it with the keyboard, your computer keys (a–k), or MIDI.

name: Correlation Meter
explanation: A phase/correlation meter with a live goniometer. Correlation is a running coefficient (exponential moving averages of L*R, L^2, R^2): +1 fully correlated (mono-safe), 0 uncorrelated, -1 fully out of phase (will cancel to silence in mono). Goniometer mode plots the standard 45-degree-rotated Mid/Side basis (mono collapses to a vertical line); Lissajous mode plots raw L/R (mono draws a diagonal instead). The meter always analyzes the true, pre-sum stereo signal - Mono Check only changes what you HEAR (sums L+R to both channels) so you can audition mono compatibility while still watching the real stereo relationship causing whatever you hear.

name: Loudness Meter
explanation: A real ITU-R BS.1770-4 / EBU R128 loudness meter. K-weighting (2 cascaded biquads, the published 48kHz coefficients) feeds 400ms gating blocks on a 100ms hop: Momentary is the latest block, Short-term is the mean of the last 3 seconds, and Integrated uses the standard's two-gate method (absolute gate at -70 LUFS, then a relative gate 10 LU below that mean) via a 701-bin histogram - the same approach the open-source reference implementation libebur128 uses. True Peak is an honestly-scoped approximation (4x linear interpolation between samples, not a full oversampling filter). Audio passes through unaltered except Input Trim and Channel Mode's Mono-sum option, which sums L+R to both channels so you can audition what summing to mono does to the reading. Reset zeroes the Integrated/Short-term history.

name: Silverbox 606
explanation: The portable analog rhythm box, modelled on the Roland TR-606: bass drum, snare, low and high tom, cymbal, open and closed hi-hat with the panel's ACCENT and six instrument-mix levels, VOLUME and TEMPO. The metals come from six free-running Schmitt oscillators (245–625 Hz) through band-passes at 3.44 and 7.1 kHz; the stock open hat has no decay knob — its length follows the tempo, and a closed hat cuts it, just like the hardware. A Mods section adds the classic hardware mods (decays, tunes, snappy) — fully left is stock. 16-step sequencer with scale 1–4, last step and an accent row, locked to your DAW.

name: Warehouse 909
explanation: A complete hybrid rhythm composer modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes. Analog bass drum (tune, level, attack, decay: a waveshaped VCO with a falling pitch contour and a separate click), snare (two synced triangle VCOs bent down over 20 ms, plus low- and high-passed noise for Tone and Snappy), three toms, rim shot and hand clap; hi-hat, crash and ride as 6-bit PCM read at the original ~30 kHz clock — the closed hat is the first third of the open hat's sample, exactly as in the hardware (the samples themselves are our own). Sequencer as the manual describes: four scales, last step, shuffle 1–7, flam with eight intervals on BD/SD/toms, a total-accent row and per-instrument accent on BD, SD, toms and closed hat, sample-locked to your DAW. MIDI on the 909's own map (36 BD, 38 SD, 42/46 hats, 49 crash, 51 ride).

name: Bridgewell 80
explanation: A complete analog rhythm composer modelled circuit-by-circuit on the Roland TR-808, from its Operation Manual and 1981 Service Notes: all 16 sounds (bass drum, snare, three toms/congas, rim shot/claves, hand clap/maracas, cowbell, cymbal, open and closed hi-hat) with every panel control — LEVEL, TONE, DECAY, SNAPPY, TUNING, the five instrument-select switches, ACCENT and MASTER VOLUME. The bass drum rings a bridged-T filter that jumps an octave for its first 4 ms and 'sighs' down in pitch as it decays; toms bend down the same way; the metals come from six free-running square oscillators. Voices are tuned and timed to Roland's own adjustment chart. Built-in 16-step sequencer with PRE-SCALE (triplets to 32nds), last step, A/AB/B variations and an accent row, locked sample-accurately to your DAW's song position. Play it from MIDI on the General-MIDI drum map (36 kick, 38 snare, 42/46 hats…); velocity 100+ is accented.

name: Colossus
explanation: Hybrid trailer strings. Every note is three ensembles at once — an octave down, unison and an octave up — each up to five detuned band-limited voices with their own drift, plus a sub, bow-hair rosin noise and a marcato bite that opens the filter. The Ostinato engine replays the held chord in rhythm, locked to your DAW's bar: 8ths, 16ths, gallop, reverse gallop, triplets, the 3-3-2 figure, dotted 8ths and 32nds, with note length, accent and swing. Evolve moves the tone over time, Tension adds a quiet minor second, Pump ducks every beat. String-body formants, tape saturation and a hall. CC1 dynamics, CC11 expression, pitch bend.

name: Aleatora
explanation: Aleatoric string textures for film and trailer sound design, played by the same physically modelled bowed-string section as Tessitura. Each key spawns a cluster of players spread by cents (optionally on a quarter-tone grid); Swarm sends every player gliding after its own random pitch targets; Rise or Fall glides the whole mass over up to 30 seconds — the trailer riser; Scratch digs the bow in with real overpressure; Shimmer adds an octave-up flautando; Pulse swells the bow in time with your DAW; Freeze holds the hall forever. Chaos scales it all. Eight articulations on C0–G0, CC1 dynamics, CC11 expression.

name: Tessitura
explanation: A physically modelled orchestral string section — no samples. Every note is bowed by up to six players, each a real-time bowed-string model (the McIntyre–Schumacher–Woodhouse waveguide with stick-slip bow friction, as in Cook & Scavone's STK) on a violin, viola, cello or bass body, with their own intonation, vibrato and bow timing, seated across the stage. Eight articulations on keyswitches C0–G0 — sustain, tremolo, pizzicato, spiccato, marcato, harmonics, sul ponticello, col legno — and the controls composers expect: CC1 dynamics (bow speed, pressure and tone together), CC11 expression, CC21 vibrato, sustain pedal, true legato (soft notes slide, hard notes change bow). Close, tree and ambient microphones into a hall.

name: Silverbox Hats
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-606 from its manual and service notes; the same model as inside Silverbox 606, on its own mixer channel. Open and closed hi-hat from the metal oscillators' upper band, bright up in the 10 kHz region. The stock open hat has no decay knob: its length follows the tempo.

name: Silverbox Cymbal
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-606 from its manual and service notes; the same model as inside Silverbox 606, on its own mixer channel. Six square oscillators through both band-passes, two VCAs on one envelope and two high-passes.

name: Silverbox Toms
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-606 from its manual and service notes; the same model as inside Silverbox 606, on its own mixer channel. Two twin-T toms with a short burst of low-passed noise rumble.

name: Silverbox Snare
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-606 from its manual and service notes; the same model as inside Silverbox 606, on its own mixer channel. A twin-T drum and high-passed noise — bright and thin, the acid-house snare. Mods: the classic pitch-down, and snappy.

name: Silverbox Kick
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-606 from its manual and service notes; the same model as inside Silverbox 606, on its own mixer channel. A short, punchy twin-T kick with a clicky edge; the stock 606 has only a level control, the mod knobs add decay and tune.

name: Warehouse Ride
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. A 6-bit ride with a bell partial, read at a tunable ~30 kHz clock, decay from the playback position.

name: Warehouse Crash
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. A 6-bit crash read at a tunable ~30 kHz clock; its decay comes from the playback position, so tuning up shortens it, like the original.

name: Warehouse Hats
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. One 6-bit sample at ~30 kHz: the closed hat plays its first third, the open hat three quarters, each shaped by its own analog decay. The sample is synthesised, the playback path is the 909's.

name: Warehouse Clap
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. Band-passed noise re-struck four times in quick succession over a reverb-like tail.

name: Warehouse Rim
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. Two ringing filters (≈500 Hz and 1.7 kHz) through a harmonics-rich VCA on a very short envelope.

name: Warehouse Toms
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. Three toms: a VCO with a falling pitch contour, a faint shell partial and a burst of tom noise. Tune, Level and Decay each.

name: Warehouse Snare
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. Two triangle VCOs (≈180 and 330 Hz) reset together and bent down over 20 ms, on separate decays; Tone opens the noise low-pass, Snappy adds the high-passed snare wires.

name: Warehouse Kick
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-909 from its Owner's Manual and Service Notes; the same model as inside Warehouse 909, on its own mixer channel. A sawtooth VCO shaped to a near-sine, swept down from several times its pitch, plus a noise-and-pulse click. Tune, Level, Attack, Decay — accent lifts and lengthens it.

name: Bridgewell Bass
explanation: The 808 bass drum as a pitched instrument, the way hip-hop and trap use it. The same bridged-T circuit as Bridgewell Kick — attack octave jump, pitch sigh, beater click — tuned to the note you play, with decay stretched to 4 s, release on note-off, glide (always or legato-only), octave, pitch bend and a drive stage for the distorted 808.

name: Bridgewell Hats
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. Open and closed hi-hat from the six-oscillator metal source's upper band, each through its own harmonics-rich VCA and high-pass. Kept together in one plugin so the closed hat can choke the open one.

name: Bridgewell Cymbal
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. Six square oscillators (205–800 Hz) summed and split into three bands with their own envelopes; Tone sets the ratio, Decay the length of the main band (350–1200 ms).

name: Bridgewell Cowbell
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. Two free-running square oscillators at 540 and 800 Hz, gated and band-passed, with the circuit's two-stage envelope: an abrupt drop after the strike, then a ringing tail.

name: Bridgewell Clap & Maracas
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. The clap is band-passed noise through a sawtooth envelope that re-fires three times before the fourth ramp is left to decay, over a slower 'reverb' envelope — the multiple-hands sound. Maracas: short high-passed noise.

name: Bridgewell Rim & Claves
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. Rim shot: two resonators (455 / 1667 Hz) through the 808's harmonics-rich 'swing' VCA on a 10 ms envelope. Claves: a single high-Q 2.5 kHz ring.

name: Bridgewell Toms
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. The three tom/conga slots. Each drum's pitch starts high and falls as it rings (the circuit's diodes), toms add a whisper of noise 'reverb'. Frequencies follow Roland's chart: toms 80–220 Hz, congas 165–455 Hz.

name: Bridgewell Snare
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. Two bridged-T resonators (238 and 476 Hz) for the drum, balanced by Tone, plus a separately enveloped high-passed noise for the snares, set by Snappy. Any MIDI note plays it.

name: Bridgewell Kick
explanation: Modelled on the Roland TR-808 from its Service Notes; the same circuit model as inside Bridgewell 80, on its own so it gets its own mixer channel. A bridged-T resonator rings at 56 Hz, jumps an octave for its first 4 ms, and sighs down in pitch as it fades — more so on accented hits. Level, Tone (the passive filter on the beater click), Decay (50 ms to a long boom), Tune. Any MIDI note plays it.

name: Antenna Lead
explanation: A theremin-style monophonic lead. A near-sine oscillator (Timbre adds the 2nd and 3rd harmonics of a real instrument) glides continuously between notes; a volume-hand envelope opens and closes the sound with velocity as hand height; slow random Drift makes pitch and level wander like an unsupported hand; vibrato fades in after a delay (mod wheel and aftertouch deepen it). Parallel formant resonators (Formant, Body) give the vocal oo-ah character, Beat Noise adds heterodyne hiss, Sub and Octave extend the range, and a small stereo room finishes it. Legato mode glides between overlapping notes.

name: Choirloft
explanation: A vocal choir and formant synthesiser. Each note is sung by up to four singers, each a glottal-style source (band-limited saw with spectral tilt set by Effort, plus breath noise) run through five parallel formant resonators. Formant frequencies, bandwidths and levels come from vowel tables for bass, tenor, alto and soprano voices and morph continuously across the vowels A-E-I-O-U, with the mod wheel pushing the morph further and Formant Shift changing apparent size. Singers differ in tuning, vibrato phase and rate and entry time (Ensemble, Human); pitch can scoop up into each note; CC11 and aftertouch shape expression. A stereo choir spread and a small hall finish it. Six notes, four singers each.

name: Cross Modulator
explanation: A meta-modulator effect: crosses the input against an internal complex carrier oscillator through one of four algorithms. Difference/XOR-Fold takes the (input minus carrier) and folds it, producing sum/difference-tone artifacts like a comparator circuit. Wavefold Cross uses the input's amplitude to drive how hard the carrier gets folded — the input controls the carrier's harmonic content rather than being folded itself. Chebyshev Cross blends the carrier through increasing Chebyshev polynomial orders as the input gets louder, adding input-dependent harmonics. Hard-Sync Cross resets the carrier's phase on the input's zero-crossings, classic oscillator hard-sync driven by whatever you feed it. Track Input blends the carrier's frequency from the Carrier Freq knob toward a rough zero-crossing pitch-follow of the input, so the carrier can lock to what you're playing instead of running free. This plugin format gives an effect one audio input, not two — so unlike a hardware meta-modulator with a second CV/audio input, this always crosses against its own internal oscillator, which is exactly how those modules behave with nothing patched into that second input anyway. Deliberately skips plain ring-modulation and vocoding — Ring Mod and Robot Voice already cover those elsewhere.

name: Engine Eight
explanation: A macro-oscillator voice: one instrument, eight selectable digital synthesis engines, all played through the same three macro knobs so switching engines never means re-learning the panel. Harmonics/Timbre/Morph mean something different per engine: Analog is a detuned 2-oscillator blend with a pulse/saw morph and sub; Fold pushes a sine through a folding waveshaper with adjustable asymmetry and a second fold stage; Chord plays a 4-voice interval set (unison through add9) off one wavetable-style oscillator with ensemble detune; Speech morphs a pulse/noise exciter through three vowel formants (A-E-I-O-U) that can track the played pitch; Granular spawns overlapping Hann-windowed grains with adjustable density, waveform and pitch scatter; Modal is a damped, dispersive Karplus-Strong string/bell pluck; Noise runs white or 'dust' impulse noise through a bank of resonators tuned to harmonics of the note; Percussion is four self-contained analog-style drum models (kick/snare/hihat/clap) selected by Harmonics. A shared glide, ADSR, resonant low-pass with envelope amount, a routable LFO (pitch/cutoff/timbre) and a width/pan output stage sit underneath every engine.

name: Modal Strike
explanation: A general-purpose modal resonator: excite it and it rings like a struck bar, a bowed rod, a blown tube, or a plucked string — one shared physical-modeling algorithm, not a dedicated instrument model. Exciter picks how energy gets in: Strike is a fast, bright noise burst (mallet); Bow is continuous, gate-sustained low-passed noise (bowed friction); Blow is continuous highpassed breath noise; Pluck is a slower, softer burst. Six parallel damped resonators are tuned to a partial set that Structure morphs from a plain harmonic stack to a stretched, inharmonic bell/bar series. Position emulates striking or plucking at a point along the body — partials whose mode has a node there get suppressed, exactly like a real string or bar. Brightness tilts how much extra damping the upper partials get; Damping sets the overall ring length. Differs from Pluckwork (a single dedicated waveguide plucked-string model for guitar/harp/koto/sitar): this is the 'hit or bow or blow anything' resonator — metal, glass, wood, membrane, string.

name: Orbit Pan
explanation: An auto-pan and tremolo unit with one LFO (sine, triangle, soft square, saw, or random sample-and-hold, with an edge-smoothing control) driving four modes: equal-power auto-pan of the stereo image; amplitude tremolo with a left/right phase offset; harmonic tremolo, where a crossover splits the signal and modulates the low and high bands in antiphase for the swirling brownface sound; and ping-pong, where left and right alternate. The rate is free (0.05 to 20 Hz) or locked to the host tempo from 1/1 down to 1/32 and phase-locked to the host beat position while the transport plays.

name: Pluckwork
explanation: A plucked-string instrument built on a digital waveguide. Each voice is a double course of strings: a delay-line loop with fractional tuning, loop low-pass (Brightness), two allpass stages of dispersion (Stiffness), an optional nonlinear bridge (Buzz, the sitar jawari), a pitch-falling Twang and a damper felt on release. Strings are struck by a comb-filtered noise burst (Pick Position, Hardness, velocity). The strings drive a four-resonator soundbox (Body Mix and Size) and eight tuned sympathetic strings, then a small stereo room. Character presets set it up as nylon or steel guitar, harp, harpsichord, koto, banjo or sitar, and every knob stays free to tweak.

name: Spectral Smear
explanation: An FFT spectral processor: a stereo short-time Fourier transform (Hann analysis and synthesis, 75% overlap, 1024/2048/4096 points) with per-bin magnitude and phase processing. Freeze holds the spectrum, with each bin keeping its measured frequency so tones sustain coherently. Sustain is a spectral hold with adjustable decay, like an infinite reverb. Blur smears magnitudes across time and across neighbouring bins. Gate drops the quietest bins. Pitch and Shift remap bins by ratio and by an absolute Hz offset. Tilt, Low Cut and High Cut are spectral EQ. Phase can be kept, randomised (whisper) or zeroed (robot), and Width decorrelates the right channel. The dry path is delayed to match the analysis latency, so Mix stays coherent.

name: Spectrum Analyzer
explanation: A 16-band real-time spectrum display. Audio passes through completely unaltered — safe to drop on a master bus without changing the sound — except for Input Trim, a real pre-analysis gain stage. A bank of 16 log-spaced (60 Hz - 16 kHz) resonant bandpass filters, one per band, each drives an attack/release envelope follower; the 16 band levels are converted to a dB scale (-60..0 dB) and streamed live to the display. Tilt adds up to +4.5 dB/octave of pink-noise-style boost to the high bands so broadband material reads flat instead of naturally sloping down, exactly like the tilt control on real hardware analyzers. Channel selects Left, Right or the L+R sum; Freeze holds the current picture for A/B comparison. 16 bands is a deliberate, not arbitrary, choice: the plugin format's DSP-to-GUI telemetry channel is a fixed 16 floats, the same budget many real hardware spectrum displays (10-31 band) work within for the same practical reason.

name: Stackhead Amp
explanation: A guitar amplifier and cabinet simulator. Signal path: input trim, noise gate, tight high-pass and bright control, a three-stage triode-style preamp (asymmetric clipping with interstage coupling filters and stage bandwidth, oversampled) in four voicings from clean to high-gain, a passive-style tone stack (bass, mid, treble), a power amp with soft push-pull saturation, supply sag and a presence shelf, then a cabinet: speaker resonances modelled as parametric peaks, a steep high roll-off, cone compression, mic position from bright on-axis to dark off-axis, and a room-blend mic distance with stereo decorrelation. Three cabinet sizes (open 1x12, 2x12, closed 4x12); the cabinet can be bypassed to feed a separate impulse-response loader.

name: Stutter Grid
explanation: A tempo-synced stutter and glitch processor. The input is captured continuously; on every grid step (1/4 to 1/32 note, locked to the host transport while it plays, otherwise the internal tempo) a seeded random draw decides what happens to that step: pass through untouched, stutter a slice (with seamless loop crossfade, per-repeat pitch ramp, decay and a falling low-pass), reverse the last step, mute it, tape-stop it, or replay it at double speed. The draw is seeded by the Seed and the step index modulo the Pattern Length, so the same glitch pattern repeats every 1, 2, 4 or 8 bars until the seed changes. Force Stutter holds the stutter on demand. Pass steps have no latency.

name: Tinebar Electric
explanation: A modal electric-piano model. A struck tine is a cantilever beam with inharmonic partials (1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.4) coupled to a tuned tonebar whose slight detune produces the slow chorus-like beating of the real instrument. A hammer burst (Hardness, velocity) excites the modes, a low thump resonator adds the felt hit, and a nonlinear pickup (Bark) turns the sine into growl on hard strikes: an asymmetric electromagnetic pickup for the tine model, a stronger electrostatic second-harmonic pickup for the reed model. Damper felt on release, preamp drive, tone, suitcase tremolo or auto-pan, key-dependent stereo width and a small room finish it. Twelve voices.

name: Waveloom
explanation: A wavetable synthesiser. Three table sets (Analog, Vocal, Digital), each of eight frames, are synthesised at start-up from harmonic spectra and stored as six band-limited octave mip levels so oscillators do not alias on the fundamental. Two oscillators scan their tables with linear morphing between frames (Position); five warp modes (none, sync, bend, mirror, pulse-width) reshape the phase; up to seven-voice unison adds detune and stereo spread; a sub oscillator and noise fill out the sound. A multimode filter (LP24, LP12, BP, HP, notch) has drive, key-track and velocity control. An amp ADSR, a modulation envelope (to Position and filter) and two LFOs (Position, filter and vibrato) shape everything over time. Eight voices.

name: Windbore
explanation: Physical-model wind instruments built from digital waveguides. Three excitation engines share one monophonic breath-controlled voice: a single-reed valve driving a bore that morphs from cylinder (clarinet, odd harmonics) to cone (saxophone, all harmonics); an air jet blowing across an open bore (flute); and a lip resonator squeezing against bore pressure (brass). Breath pressure has attack and release, noise, vibrato and is driven by velocity, aftertouch and CC2/CC11. A tone-hole low-pass, bell/body resonance, glide, legato and a small room complete it. Character presets set clarinet, saxophone, oboe, flute, trumpet or trombone; every control stays free.

name: Wobble Deck
explanation: A tape and cassette degrader. The signal runs through a modulated delay line that wanders: slow wow, faster flutter (both depend on tape speed) and random drift, with a stereo link control. Random dropouts dip the level like oxide loss. A tape-style asymmetric saturator and a fast squash compressor follow, then the head: head bump (low resonance), age- and speed-dependent high-frequency loss, azimuth error (a small delay and treble loss between channels), tape hiss and mains hum. The dry path is delay-matched so Mix never combs. Three tape speeds change the bandwidth, hiss and wobble character.

name: Fourfold FM
explanation: A four-operator FM instrument in the style of the Yamaha OPN2/OPM sound chips. Four sine operators are wired by the chip's eight connection algorithms, with self-feedback on operator 1. Every operator has total level in 0.75 dB steps, frequency multiple, detune, key-scale rate and a five-stage chip envelope (attack rate, decay-1 rate and level, decay-2 rate, release rate) computed in dB. A shared LFO (eight rates) applies AM (per-operator enable, four depths) and FM (eight depths) with the mod wheel adding vibrato. Each operator can also switch to OPL-style half, absolute and quarter-pulse sine shapes. DAC grit adds the converter's crunch; eight voices spread across the stereo field.

name: Cartridge Four
explanation: An 8-bit console sound instrument modelled on the Ricoh 2A03 audio unit. Two pulse channels have the chip's 8-step duty sequences (12.5/25/50/75 %), 4-bit volume, a hardware-style 240 Hz decay envelope with loop, a sweep unit, vibrato, duty animation and chord arpeggios; a triangle channel plays its 32-step 4-bit staircase; a noise channel runs a 15-bit LFSR (long/short mode, the 16-entry period table, envelope, key tracking); a DPCM channel plays delta-modulated kick, snare and tom. Everything goes through the console's nonlinear mixer and output filter chain (Famicom or NES), with optional timer-period pitch quantisation. Notes in C1-B1 play drums (DPCM and noise percussion); other notes are pitched, layered on all channels or assigned across them (Poly).

name: Chiptrio
explanation: A three-voice home-computer sound-chip instrument modelled on the architecture of the MOS 6581/8580. Each voice has a phase-accumulator oscillator with triangle, sawtooth, pulse and LFSR-noise waveforms (any combination, combined by bitwise AND), pulse width, ring modulation and hard sync in the chip's 1-2-3-1 ring, and an 8-bit ADSR using the chip's sixteen attack/decay/release times. One shared 12 dB state-variable filter (low/band/high in any mix, per-voice routing) has a 6581 mode with input overload and softer cutoff and a clean 8580 mode. Play Poly, Unison or Arp (held notes cycle at chip speed). PWM, vibrato/mod wheel, lo-fi bit and clock reduction and unison detune round it out.

name: Cross-Talk
explanation: A two-signal cross-modulator and 16-band vocoder. The modulator is the right input (or the mono sum); the carrier is an internal four-note oscillator chord (Pitch, Chord, Waveform saw>pulse>noise, Detune) or the left input. Algorithm sweeps one continuous path through crossfade, cross-fold, ring modulation, bitwise AND/XOR/OR, comparator and a channel vocoder, with Timbre re-mapped by each stage. The vocoder has steep two-stage band-passes, formant shift, band width, attack/release followers, a gate, freeze and modulator sibilance. Drive, stereo width and output level finish it.

name: Polyhedra
explanation: A nine-engine macro voice with a low-pass gate. Engine selects the source: analog saw/pulse pair, FM, wavefolder, 12-harmonic additive, Karplus-Strong string, inharmonic bell, resonant noise/dust, vowel formants or a pitch-swept kick. Harmonics, Timbre and Morph are re-mapped by each engine to its three most musical axes. A struck-or-gated envelope drives loudness and the gate filter (Color); envelope, LFO, velocity and aftertouch can all move Timbre/Morph. Sub, Air noise, stereo spread across eight voices, vibrato (mod wheel), pitch bend, drive and a ping-pong echo complete the voice.

name: Glasswork
explanation: A modal-resonator instrument. Each voice is a bank of up to 24 resonators tuned to a partial series that morphs from vibrating string through free bar and cast bell to singing bowl (Structure, with Stretch for inharmonicity). A mallet strikes the modes (Hardness, Strike, Position); Bow and Breath exciters sustain them while a key is held (Flow shapes the attack). Brightness, Damping and Tilt control mode gains and frequency-dependent decay; a detuned twin bank per voice gives Width. Mod wheel and aftertouch add vibrato and bow pressure, pitch bend, a small stereo reverb and drive finish it. Eight voices.

name: Shard Sequencer
explanation: A 16-step granular slice sequencer. Incoming audio is captured into a rolling (or Held) buffer cut into 16 slices across a 1/2/4/8-beat Capture window; a step sequence locked to the DAW playhead (free-running when stopped) fires shards from any slice. Each step sets Slice (or rest), Pitch (±24 st), Reverse, Ratchet (1–4 hits) and Gate (25–100%). Global Steps, Division (1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32, 1/8T), Swing, Chance, Jitter, Fade, Tone, Crush, Spread, Duck (dry gate while shards play), Mix and Level. Hold freezes the capture into a locked loop for beat-repeat style glitching.

name: Prism Shift
explanation: A pitch-tracking granular harmonizer. Five granular pitch-shifting voices (a Main voice plus four harmony voices, each with Level, Interval, Fine, Pan and Delay) read one delay line through crossfaded swept taps. A normalised-autocorrelation pitch detector follows the played note; in Diatonic mode the intervals are scale degrees in the chosen Key and Scale (major, minor, dorian, mixolydian, lydian, phrygian, harmonic minor, minor pentatonic) so thirds and fifths are major or minor as the key demands, while Chromatic mode uses plain semitones. Correct pulls the tracked note onto the scale, Lock sizes each grain to an even multiple of the detected pitch period so the overlapping taps stay in phase, Glide gives tuned portamento between notes, Humanize adds per-voice drift, and Feedback stacks the harmonies into cascading chords.

name: Nebula Freeze
explanation: A live granular texture processor with freeze. Audio is captured into an ~8 s stereo buffer and resprayed by a pool of 64 grains with 4-point Hermite interpolation. Position/Spray choose where grains start, Size and Density set grain length and rate, Chaos slides spawn timing from metronomic to Poisson, Texture morphs the window from percussive through Hann to a flat-topped plateau, Pitch/Jitter transpose (optionally snapped to octaves, fifths, minor pentatonic, major or whole-tone), Reverse plays grains backwards at random, Spread pans each grain. Freeze locks the buffer so it becomes a playable texture; Feedback recirculates the cloud; Tone tilts, Degrade adds sample-rate and bit reduction, and a diffuse reverb tail blooms behind it.

name: Acid Bass
explanation: A monophonic squelch-bass synth modelled control-for-control on the Roland TB-303 Bass Line (Owner's Manual read cover to cover). ONE oscillator with the WAVEFORM switch picking the two classic 303 waves — sawtooth or square, polyBLEP band-limited — and a TUNING master tune (+/-500 cents). The signature filter is an 18 dB/oct (3-pole) diode-ladder-style resonant low-pass with CUTOFF FREQ and RESONANCE (near maximum it pushes toward self-oscillation). A single decay-only envelope (DECAY sets its time; the manual notes both the volume and the tone fade together) sweeps the filter by the ENV MOD amount. The ACCENT circuit boosts level, adds a fast extra resonant filter sweep and the characteristic accent wow, and accumulates across consecutive accents. SLIDE is a fixed-time legato glide between tied steps. A built-in 16-step, 40-300 BPM sequencer (each step carrying pitch, accent, slide and rest) auto-plays a recognisable acid line; the transport RUN/WRITE bits are packed into one host parameter and the panel drives recording via note events.

name: Additive
explanation: A polyphonic additive (Fourier) synthesizer modelled on the Kawai K5 (Owner's Manual, read cover to cover). Every voice is a genuine harmonic bank: TWO independent sources (S1/S2), each summing 64 sinusoidal partials, faithfully echoing the K5's dual DHG (Digital Harmonic Generator) that spreads 126 harmonics over two halves. Rather than 126 raw sliders, the harmonic spectrum is sculpted by musically meaningful MACROS per source: a harmonic PROFILE selector (saw 1/n, square odd-1/n, pulse, triangle, organ octaves, resonant) that seeds the bank; a bipolar spectral TILT/brightness slope; an ODD/EVEN partial balance; a DENSITY control over how many partials sound; and a DFT-style FORMANT emphasis (peak frequency, width and amount) that pushes energy into a harmonic band. The K5's four six-stage DHG amplitude envelopes are modelled as three HARMONIC BAND envelopes (low/mid/high, attack+decay) so the spectrum morphs over the life of the note — the signature evolving K5 timbre. Each source then passes through a DDF (Dynamic Digital Filter: spectral low-pass over the harmonic bank with resonance, its own attack/decay envelope and keyboard scaling) and a DDA (Digital Dynamic Amplifier: ADSR amplitude contour). Global: a DFG pitch envelope, a shared LFO (triangle/saw/ramp/square/random) routable to pitch, spectrum, amplitude and formant with optional key sync; S1/S2 balance, S2 coarse tune and detune (Twin-mode beating), master tune, portamento, pitch-bend wheel with range, mod-wheel vibrato, aftertouch pressure and volume. Mode, key-sync and DDF key-track switches are bit-packed into one mask parameter which the panel decodes into individual switches. Pure algorithm, allocation-free process(); the harmonic amplitude arrays are recomputed at control rate and summed per-sample by a complex-recurrence sine bank so 128 partials over 6 voices stay real-time.

name: Analog Poly
explanation: A five-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled feature-for-feature on the Sequential Prophet-5 Rev 4 (User's Guide v1.3). Per voice: Oscillator A with simultaneous sawtooth and variable-width square/pulse waves (polyBLEP) and hard SYNC to Oscillator B; Oscillator B with simultaneous sawtooth, triangle and pulse waves, FINE tune, LO FREQ (turns it into a per-voice LFO) and KEYBOARD-off switches; frequency knobs stepped in semitones over four octaves; a mixer for Osc A, Osc B and white noise; a resonant self-oscillating 24 dB low-pass filter with the Rev 4 REV switch selecting two genuinely different voicings (Rev 1/2 SSM 2040-style: rawer, brighter tap, near-linear envelope segments; Rev 3 CEM 3320-style: saturating ladder with exponential envelope curves), envelope amount, and off/half/full keyboard tracking; dedicated filter and amplifier ADSRs with per-envelope velocity switches and the classic RELEASE switch (off = fast release on both envelopes); POLY MOD routing the filter envelope and audio-rate Oscillator B into Osc A frequency (exponential FM), Osc A pulse width and filter cutoff; an LFO with saw/triangle/square shape switches (any combination; saw and square positive-only, triangle bipolar, 0.022-500 Hz); the WHEEL-MOD section with an LFO-to-noise source-mix knob and Freq A / Freq B / PW A / PW B / Filter destination switches, ridden by the mod wheel on top of the LFO INITIAL AMOUNT; the VINTAGE knob (4 = tight modern Rev4 ... 1 = loose Rev1) scaling per-voice random spread of oscillator pitch, filter cutoff, envelope times and amp gain plus slow drift; GLIDE; UNISON with 1-5 voice stacking, detune 0-8, chord memory and LO/LO-retrig/LAST/LAST-retrig key priority; spring-loaded pitch wheel with 1-12 semitone bend range, mod wheel, aftertouch (pressure) routable to filter and/or LFO amount, MASTER TUNE (about a semitone each way) and the A-440 reference tone. Switch groups are bit-packed into single host parameters; the panel shows every individual switch.

name: Brass Eight
explanation: An eight-voice, sixteen-oscillator polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled control-for-control on the Oberheim OB-Xa (OB-Xa Owner's Manual, 3rd Ed., April 1982, read cover to cover). Each of the eight voices is a complete synth with two VCOs, two selectable low-pass filters (a 2-pole and a 4-pole), two ADSR envelopes and a VCA. OSC 1 has an octave FREQUENCY control (4-octave range) and independent SAW and PULSE waveform switches that sum additively. OSC 2 has a coarse FREQUENCY (5-octave, half-step), a bipolar DETUNE (+/-50 cents, flat or sharp of OSC 1), and its own SAW/PULSE switches; SYNC hard-locks OSC 2 to OSC 1 for the classic timbral sweep, and F-ENV routes the Filter Envelope to OSC 2's pitch (amount set by the filter MODULATION control, up to +1 octave). A shared PULSE WIDTH control sets both oscillators' duty (50% square fully CCW, thin/nasal CW). The programmable MODULATION section is a LFO (SINE / SQUARE / SAMPLE&HOLD, ~0.1-20 Hz) with a FREQUENCY DEPTH routable to OSC 1 / OSC 2 / FILTER and a PULSE-WIDTH DEPTH routable to OSC 1 / OSC 2. The FILTER section both selects the sound sources into the filter (OSC 1, OSC 2 at HALF or FULL level, pink NOISE) and shapes them: FREQUENCY, RESONANCE (raises level in 2-pole, lowers it in 4-pole), MODULATION (filter-env amount), a 2-POLE/4-POLE slope switch (the OB-Xa signature: 12 dB/oct bright vs 24 dB/oct full) and keyboard TRACK. Two four-stage ADSR envelopes drive the Filter and the Loudness (VCA). Performance: polyphonic PORTAMENTO with linear/quantized and offset options, UNISON (low-note-priority 8-voice stack), HOLD latch, a PITCH BEND lever (OSC-2-only and NARROW +/-whole-step vs +/-octave switches), a MOD lever that fades LFO vibrato in, master TRANSPOSE (+/-octave), MASTER TUNE and VOLUME. Switch groups are bit-packed into single host parameters; the panel decodes and shows every individual switch. SPLIT / DOUBLE dual-keyboard modes, chord-memory transposition, auto-tune and the cassette/patch-memory system are host or hardware concerns and are out of scope (single Whole-mode patch).

name: Cinematic Poly
explanation: An eight-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled on the Yamaha CS-80 (Instruction Manual, read cover to cover). Every voice is TWO complete, independent synthesizer channels (I and II) mixed together, giving the CS-80's huge, layered sound. Each channel has its own VCO (simultaneous sawtooth and variable-width square/pulse with pulse-width modulation, plus white noise and a pure sine that bypasses the filter), a resonant HIGH-PASS filter and a resonant LOW-PASS filter in series (each with its own cutoff and RESONANCE 'Q'), a five-stage IL-AL-A-D-R filter envelope unique to the CS-80 that moves both filter cutoffs (Initial Level below the steady cutoff, Attack Level above it, then Attack / Decay / Release times), and an A-D-S-R amplifier envelope with its own VCF/SINE mix levels. The two channels have independent FEET (16'/8'/5-1/3'/4'/2-2/3'/2') tunings and a DETUNE II control, blended by the MIX I-II balance. Global performance and modifier sections: a SUB OSCILLATOR (sine / sawtooth / inverted-saw / square / noise / external function, SPEED, and VCO / VCF depths) for vibrato, wah and growl; a RING MODULATOR (modulation amount, speed, depth); a stereo TREMOLO/CHORUS; PORTAMENTO/GLISSANDO; SUSTAIN; overall BRILLIANCE and RESONANCE; shared PWM SPEED; master PITCH tune; and the CS-80's signature performance controls: velocity PITCHBEND and INITIAL-TOUCH brilliance, polyphonic AFTER-TOUCH routed to brilliance, level and vibrato/pitch, plus the velvet PITCH RIBBON. Switch groups (each channel's square/saw waveform enables and the tremolo, portamento and sustain mode switches) are bit-packed into one mask parameter; the panel decodes and shows every individual switch. The tone-selector presets, memory panel, foot-switch assigners and keyboard level/brilliance scaling are host/hardware concerns and out of scope.

name: Duo Synth
explanation: A duophonic analog lead/bass synthesizer modelled feature-for-feature on the ARP Odyssey (Owner's Manual, Second Edition, March 1976). The keyboard is 2-voice paraphonic: the lowest held key drives VCO 1 (low-note priority) and the highest held key drives VCO 2 (high-note priority), exactly as the specifications state, so two keys sound as two distinct pitches while a single key locks both oscillators together. Two VCOs each offer sawtooth or square/pulse with a variable PULSE WIDTH (50%->5%) and PULSE-WIDTH MODULATION; VCO 1 has a low-frequency (LF) mode; VCO 2 has hard SYNC to VCO 1. The signature ARP modulation matrix is a set of amount sliders each fed by a two-position source switch: VCO1+2 FM (Sine-LFO / S&H), VCO2 FM (Sine-LFO / ADSR), VCO1 PWM and VCO2 PWM (Sine-LFO / ADSR), VCF FM x2 (Sine-LFO / S&H and ADSR / AR) and VCF keyboard tracking (Kbd / S&H). Sources: a LOW FREQUENCY OSCILLATOR with simultaneous sine and square outputs, a SAMPLE & HOLD (its own 2-input mixer, LFO- or keyboard-clocked, with output LAG) and the two envelopes. AUDIO MIXER blends VCO1, VCO2 and a third channel switchable between white/pink NOISE and the RING MODULATOR (VCO1xVCO2). The self-oscillating 4-pole low-pass VCF (Q to 30, resonance to self-oscillation) is preceded by a non-resonant HIGH-PASS FILTER. The VCA is driven by the ADSR, the AR or a straight GATE (drone), with an initial-GAIN slider. Performance: PORTAMENTO, master TUNE, +/-2-octave TRANSPOSE, +/-1-octave PITCH BEND with centre dead-zone, PPC vibrato depth, a REPEAT switch (Kbd gate / Auto-repeat / Kbd-repeat that lets the LFO retrigger the envelopes) and VOLUME. Switch groups are bit-packed into two mask parameters so the whole instrument fits the 64-param host pool; the panel decodes every individual switch.

name: Fat Mono
explanation: A monophonic analog synthesizer modelled control-for-control on the Moog Minimoog Model D (User's Manual Version 2, read cover to cover). Three oscillators, each with six waveforms (triangle, triangle-sawtooth hybrid — reverse sawtooth on oscillator 3 — sawtooth, square, wide pulse, narrow pulse) and six ranges (LO, 32', 16', 8', 4', 2'); oscillators 2 and 3 fine-tune +/-7 semitones; OSC. 3 CONTROL switch releases oscillator 3 from the keyboard for drones and free-running modulation. Five-source mixer (Osc 1/2/3, white/pink noise, external input) with per-source on/off rocker switches and the famous no-cable feedback overload drive (scaled by Main Output Volume, per the manual). Modulation bus: OSC. 3/FILTER EG and NOISE/LFO source switches, MODULATION MIX knob, mod wheel, OSCILLATOR MODULATION and FILTER MODULATION switches; when WHITE noise is selected the mod source is pink noise, when PINK is selected it is red noise (manual p.21). Dedicated LFO (0.05-200 Hz) with the push/pull triangle/square shape switch. 24 dB/oct ladder low-pass with Cutoff (-4..+4), self-oscillating Emphasis, Amount of Contour (0-4 octaves), and KEYBOARD CONTROL 1 (1/3) and 2 (2/3) tracking switches. Filter and Loudness contours (Attack/Decay/Sustain) with the left-hand DECAY switch that re-uses decay time as release (off = abrupt release). Glide knob + switch (1 ms - 10 s per octave), spring-loaded pitch wheel (+/-7 semitones = a fifth, manual p.24), low/high/last note priority and multi-trigger vs legato single-trigger (Global Settings p.47), A-440 reference tuner, Main Output switch, master TUNE, and the reissue's velocity-to-loudness and after-pressure-to-filter patch routes. Switch groups are bit-packed; the panel shows every individual rocker.

name: FM Tines
explanation: A 16-voice polyphonic 6-operator FM synthesizer modelled on the Yamaha DX7 (Operating Manual, read cover to cover). Every voice is a genuine FM tone generator: six sine-wave OPERATORS, each with its own frequency (ratio or fixed), output level, detune and multi-stage envelope, wired together by the full table of 32 ALGORITHMS (the exact DX7 carrier/modulator topologies, including the per-algorithm feedback operator). Carriers are summed to the output; modulators phase-modulate their targets to synthesise the DX7's metallic, bell-like harmonics; the FEEDBACK operator adds noise and brightness. A global LFO (triangle / saw-down / saw-up / square / sine / sample-and-hold, with SPEED, DELAY, PMD pitch-mod depth, AMD amplitude-mod depth, key sync and pitch/amp modulation sensitivity) provides vibrato and tremolo; a PITCH EG bends pitch on the attack; and a full performance section covers TRANSPOSE, MASTER TUNE, POLY/MONO, PORTAMENTO (full-time / fingered, with glissando), PITCH BEND range and wheel, and the DX7's four modulation controllers (modulation wheel, breath, after-touch pressure) each routable to pitch, amplitude or EG bias. Operator on/off, oscillator fixed-frequency mode, poly/mono, portamento and the whole controller routing matrix are bit-packed into two mask parameters; the panel decodes and shows every individual switch. The per-operator envelope is a musical 4-stage A-D-S-R compaction of the DX7's R1-4/L1-4 rate/level EG; keyboard level/rate scaling, per-operator velocity sensitivity and the foot controller are folded into global behaviour or out of scope (see README).

name: Jove Eight
explanation: An eight-voice, sixteen-oscillator polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled control-for-control on the Roland Jupiter-8 (JP-8 Owner's Manual, read cover to cover). Each voice has two VCOs: VCO-1 (triangle / sawtooth / variable pulse / square, ranges 16'-2') with a CROSS MOD slider that FM/ring-modulates its pitch from VCO-2; and VCO-2 (sine / sawtooth / variable pulse / noise, quantized ranges 16'-2', FINE tune +/-50 cents, a NORMAL/LOW-FREQ switch that turns it into a sub-audio modulator, and a SYNC switch that hard-syncs it to VCO-1). The VCO MODULATOR routes the LFO and ENV-1 to the pitch of VCO-1 / BOTH / VCO-2, and drives PULSE WIDTH MOD in MANUAL / LFO / ENV-1 mode. A rotary SOURCE MIX balances the two VCOs into a non-resonant -6 dB/oct High-Pass Filter and then the signature VCF: resonant low-pass with a -12 dB/oct vs -24 dB/oct SLOPE switch, ENV MOD (with an ENV-1/ENV-2 selector), LFO MOD and 0-120% KEY FOLLOW. The VCA is driven by ENV-2 with a four-position LFO-tremolo depth. Two complete four-stage ADSR envelopes: ENV-1 (assignable, with a KEY FOLLOW time-scaler and a NORMAL/INVERSE POLARITY switch) and ENV-2 (with KEY FOLLOW), A 1ms-5s, D/R 1ms-10s. The LFO offers sine / sawtooth / square / random(S&H) waveforms, 0.05-40 Hz, and a DELAY that fades it in per note. Full performance section: polyphonic PORTAMENTO (off/on/upper), a center-sprung BENDER routable to VCO-1 / VCO-2 / VCF with independent bend-sensitivity, and an auxiliary LFO-MOD touch pad with RISE TIME and VCO/VCF depths. Assigner: POLY-1 / POLY-2 / SOLO / UNISON (8-voice stack). A 1-4 octave UP / DOWN / U&D / RANDOM arpeggiator with internal rate and HOLD. Eight-voice polyphony. Switch groups are bit-packed into single host parameters; the panel decodes and shows every individual switch. Dual/Split two-patch key modes and the tape/patch-memory system are host concerns and out of scope (Whole mode single patch).

name: Mono Spark
explanation: A monophonic analog synthesizer modelled control-for-control on the Roland SH-101 (Owner's Manual read cover to cover). ONE VCO with a 16'/8'/4'/2' RANGE selector whose SAW and PULSE waveforms are produced simultaneously (polyBLEP band-limited) and mixed in the SOURCE MIXER alongside a three-mode SUB OSCILLATOR (1 oct down square / 2 oct down square / 2 oct down narrow pulse) and white NOISE, each with its own level fader. Pulse width is set by the PW fader with a PWM MODE switch (MANUAL / LFO / ENV) and the VCO MOD fader adds LFO to pitch. The signature 4-pole resonant low-pass VCF self-oscillates at maximum RES and has CUTOFF FREQ, ENV depth, MOD (LFO) depth and KYBD key-follow. The VCA is switchable between the envelope and a plain GATE. A single ADSR ENVELOPE (Attack 1.5 ms-4 s, Decay/Release 2 ms-10 s) shapes the VCF, VCA and (in ENV mode) the pulse width, with a GATE+TRIG / GATE / LFO trigger switch. The MODULATOR is an LFO/S&H (0.1-30 Hz) with triangle, square, random and noise shapes routed to VCO pitch and VCF. Full performance section: PORTAMENTO with OFF/ON/AUTO mode, TRANSPOSE L/M/H octave switch, master TUNE (+/-50 cents), VOLUME, the BENDER lever with independent VCO and VCF bend-sensitivity and the mod-grip push that adds LFO vibrato/growl (LFO MOD depth). The SH-101 signature auto-ARPEGGIO (up / up&down / down) and the built-in step SEQUENCER (record via note events, rests and legato ties, up to 64 steps, 40-300 BPM) are both implemented; a HOLD latch sustains held notes. Switch groups are decoded and shown individually on the panel; the transport bits (arp / seq play / seq record / hold) are packed into one host parameter.

name: Nova Six
explanation: A six-voice programmable polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled control-for-control on the Roland Juno-106 (Owner's Manual, read cover to cover). One digitally-controlled oscillator per voice producing sawtooth and a variable-width pulse SIMULTANEOUSLY (independent on/off switches, polyBLEP band-limited), plus a square sub-oscillator one octave down and white noise, all mixed per voice; 16'/8'/4' RANGE selector. PWM with the MANUAL/LFO mode switch (manual = the PW knob sets width, LFO = the LFO modulates it and the knob sets depth). A 4-position non-resonant High-Pass Filter (0 boosts the lows, 1 is flat, 2/3 progressively cut the lows). A resonant 4-pole low-pass VCF that self-oscillates at maximum resonance, with cutoff, an ENV amount knob and its +/- polarity switch, an LFO amount knob and a 0-100% key-follow knob. A VCA with the ENV/GATE control-signal switch and a level knob. A single ADSR envelope (Attack 1.5 ms-3 s, Decay/Release 1.5 ms-12 s, Sustain 0-100%) shared by the VCF and, in ENV mode, the VCA. A triangle LFO (0.1-30 Hz) with a DELAY that fades it in, feeding DCO pitch (vibrato), pulse width and the VCF. The famous Juno stereo bucket-brigade CHORUS with all three positions (I, II and both I+II). Full performance section: portamento with its time knob and on/off switch, the bend lever with independent DCO and VCF bend-sensitivity knobs (DCO up to +/-1 octave) and forward-push LFO vibrato with its own depth knob, POLY 1 / POLY 2 / SOLO (unison) assign modes and +/-1 octave key transpose. Switch groups are bit-packed into single host parameters; the panel decodes and shows every individual switch.

name: Oberon
explanation: An eight-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled control-for-control on the original 1979 Oberheim OB-X (OB-X Owner's Manual, 2nd Ed., 2nd Printing, June 1980). Each of the eight voices is a complete synth with two VCOs, a single SEM-derived 2-pole (12 dB/oct) resonant low-pass filter, two full ADSR envelopes and a VCA. This is the FIRST OB-X, NOT the later OB-Xa: it has ONLY the 2-pole filter (no selectable 4-pole slope), a smoother SEM-flavoured resonance and no filter-envelope-to-oscillator routing. CONTROL: polyphonic PORTAMENTO, UNISON (low-note-priority detuned stack), OSC 2 DETUNE (flat/sharp of OSC 1) and MASTER TUNE. MODULATION: one LFO (SINE / SQUARE / SAMPLE&HOLD, ~0.1-20 Hz) with a FREQUENCY DEPTH routable to OSC 1 / OSC 2 / FILTER and a PULSE-WIDTH DEPTH routable to OSC 1 / OSC 2. OSCILLATORS: OSC 1 and OSC 2 each have a continuous FREQUENCY control (per the manual, ~11 o'clock = one octave up) plus independent SAW and PULSE waveform switches summed additively; a shared PULSE WIDTH control; SYNC hard-locks OSC 2 to OSC 1. FILTER: the classic OB-X mixer buttons select sources into the filter (OSC 1 on/off, OSC 2 off/half/full, NOISE on/off), FREQUENCY, RESONANCE, MODULATION (filter-env amount) and keyboard TRACK (100% or off). Two ADSR envelopes drive the Filter and the Loudness (VCA). Performance: PITCH and MODULATION levers (the mod lever fades LFO vibrato in), a programmable BEND RANGE, a stereo PAN SPREAD echoing the OB-X's per-voice pan pots, HOLD latch, VOLUME. Switch groups are bit-packed into single host parameters; the panel decodes and shows every individual switch. AUTO auto-tune, the 32-program cassette/programmer memory and CHORD memory transposition are host or hardware concerns and are out of scope.

name: Patch Mono
explanation: A semi-modular monophonic synthesizer modelled behaviour-for-behaviour on the Korg MS-20 (Owner's Manual read cover to cover). Two VCOs: VCO-1 (32'/16'/8'/4' SCALE) offers Triangle / Sawtooth / variable-width Rectangle (PW knob) / White-noise waveforms; VCO-2 (16'/8'/4'/2' SCALE) offers Sawtooth / Square / narrow Pulse / Ring-modulator waveforms with a +/-1 octave PITCH detune. MASTER TUNE and PORTAMENTO are global; a VCO MIXER sets VCO-1 and VCO-2 levels. The signature Korg-35 dual filters run in series - a resonant, self-oscillating HIGH-PASS FILTER then a resonant, self-oscillating LOW-PASS FILTER, each with CUTOFF FREQUENCY and PEAK. FREQUENCY MODULATION routes MG/T.EXT and EG1/EXT to VCO pitch; CUTOFF FREQUENCY MODULATION routes MG/T.EXT and EG2/EXT independently to the HPF and the LPF. The MG (Modulation Generator) is an LFO with a WAVE FORM morph (falling ramp -> triangle -> rising ramp, plus a rectangle output) and FREQUENCY. EG1 is a DELAY / ATTACK / RELEASE modulation envelope; EG2 is a HOLD / ATTACK / DECAY / SUSTAIN / RELEASE envelope driving the VCA and (via the mod section) the filters. A Sample & Hold (noise clocked by the MG rectangle) and an EXTERNAL SIGNAL PROCESSOR (band-pass pre-amp + envelope follower + frequency-to-voltage pitch converter, normalled to the internal signal) feed the patch bay. The PATCH BAY is a compact 4-cord routing matrix: any source (MG-tri, MG-rect, EG1, EG2, S&H, Noise, Wheel, Kbd-CV, ESP-Env, ESP-Pitch) patches to any destination (Pitch, VCO-2 Pitch, PW, HPF, LPF, VCA, MG-Rate) with its own amount, exactly like re-patching the MS-20's jack field. A programmable CONTROL WHEEL with dedicated pitch and cutoff sensitivity completes the performance section. Monophonic, last-note priority.

name: Seer Six
explanation: A six-voice polyphonic analog synthesizer modelled feature-for-feature on the Sequential Prophet-6 (Operation Manual 2.1). Per voice: two VCOs with continuously-variable waveshape (triangle - sawtooth - variable-width pulse), oscillator 1 hard sync, a triangle sub-octave, white noise, a resonant 4-pole low-pass and a resonant 2-pole high-pass filter sharing one ADSR filter envelope (bipolar amounts, velocity switches, off/half/full key tracking), an ADSR amplifier envelope with amount and velocity, Slop vintage-drift, Glide with all four modes (fixed rate / fixed time, plus legato variants), an LFO with five waveshapes (plus the hidden noise shape at full frequency on Random), clock sync and six destinations, Poly Mod (filter envelope and osc 2 into osc 1 freq/shape/PW and both filters), full Aftertouch section driven by the Pressure control, Unison with 1-6 voice stacking, chord memory and all six key-assign modes, Pan Spread, stereo analog-style Distortion, a dual 24-bit effects chain (A: BBD, digital delay, chorus, three phasers, ring mod, two flangers; B adds hall, room, plate and spring reverbs) with clock-synced delays, a full arpeggiator (5 modes, 1-3 octaves, 10 clock divisions incl. dotted/swing/triplet, Hold relatch), a 64-step polyphonic sequencer with rests, ties and key transpose, plus spring-loaded pitch wheel (0-12 semitone range) and mod wheel. Switch groups are bit-packed into single host parameters; the panel shows every individual switch.

name: Quasar
explanation: An organismic patchable mono synth-voice for the experimentally minded - a wild instrument that pushes back. Two oscillators cross-modulate with through-zero FM and a feedback path, so small patch moves bloom into clangy, unpredictable, living textures. A resonant ladder low-pass, snappy ADSR, free LFO, sample & hold and noise round it out. Fully patchable: a 5x4 modulation matrix (LFO, Env, S&H, Noise, Osc2 into Pitch, Cutoff, PWM and Chaos) whose routing amounts are real parameters - cabling a source to a destination turns that amount up, so the patch you see is the patch you hear. Normalled Env-to-Cutoff and a touch of LFO-to-PWM. Not for straight subtractive sounds - for instruments that surprise you.

name: Vox Shifter
explanation: A formant-aware vocal pitch shifter in the PSOLA / phase-vocoder family. A twin-grain crossfaded delay-line pitch shifter moves the pitch (Shift, plus/minus 12 semitones) click-free, while an independent Formant control sweeps a pair of resonant vowel formants over the shifted voice, so you can pitch a voice up without the chipmunk formant collapse, or slide the formants for gender and vowel morphs. Mix blends dry and wet; Output trims level. Controls: Shift, Formant, Mix, Output.

name: Blue Flanger
explanation: A deep, resonant, wide-stereo flanger in the Boss BF-2 lineage. Distinct from the factory's other flangers by its lush, watery voice: a long swept fractional delay (~0.3-12 ms) with a strong resonant positive Feedback that can ring into metallic territory, and a stereo Width control that offsets the LFO between the left and right channels for a wide underwater spread. A triangle LFO sweeps the delay around a Manual base time. Controls: Rate, Depth, Feedback, Manual, Width and Mix.

name: Analog Bucket
explanation: A generic bucket-brigade (BBD) model: a short, dark, companded delay that doubles as a chorus/vibrato. A modulated BBD delay line with progressively darker repeats and gentle compander grit — at short times with high Mod it's a lush chorus, at longer times a warm analog echo. Controls: Time, Feedback, Mod (chorus depth), Tone (BBD darkness) and Mix.

name: Soft Opto
explanation: A smooth optical leveling amplifier (generic opto-compressor model). A slow photocell-style detector gives gentle, program-dependent gain reduction with a soft knee and a touch of warmth — gentler and slower than the factory's other compressors. Controls: Threshold, Ratio, Makeup, Tone (post tilt) and Mix.

name: Vocal Plate
explanation: A bright, dense studio plate reverb in the EMT 140 lineage — the classic vocal and snare plate, brighter and longer than an algorithmic Dattorro plate. An input diffusion chain (four series allpasses) feeds a lightly-modulated figure-of-eight tank (two allpasses and two long delays with high-frequency damping) for a lush, shimmering metallic-to-smooth tail. Controls: dry/wet Mix, Decay, Tone (brightness), Pre-Delay and plate Size.

name: Flutter Echo
explanation: A physically-modelled tape delay that foregrounds the wow and flutter of an unstable tape transport. The read head is modulated by a slow wow LFO plus a faster flutter LFO with a little drift, so every repeat is audibly pitch-warbled; each pass through the loop adds tape saturation and high-frequency loss, so echoes darken and degrade as they stack. The Warble control scales the modulation from subtle vintage warmth to seasick wobble. Controls: Time, Feedback, Warble, Tone and dry/wet Mix.

name: Glass Chorus
explanation: A pristine hi-fi stereo chorus/flanger combo. Two fractional delay lines (one per channel) are read with linear interpolation and modulated by quadrature LFOs so the left and right voices sweep in counter-phase for a wide, glassy stereo image. A single Mode control morphs the effect from a lush, gently detuned multi-voice chorus into a short, sweeping flanger comb; the Feedback control adds the resonant flange whoosh, Width spreads the stereo voices and Depth/Rate shape the sweep. The signal path stays clean with no saturation or grit. Controls: Rate, Depth, Mode, Feedback, Width and dry/wet Mix.

name: Clip Stage
explanation: A clean, transparent soft-clip saturator and drive stage — built for warmth, glue and gentle level control rather than grind. A makeup-compensated Drive feeds a selectable transfer curve: DIODE gives a symmetric soft knee with odd harmonics, while TUBE adds a small bias for asymmetric, even-harmonic warmth (an internal DC blocker removes the resulting offset). A subtle Tone tilt opens or darkens the top, an output Trim sets level, and a parallel Mix blends the saturated signal back against the dry. Controls: Drive, Curve (diode/tube), Tone, Trim and Mix.

name: Valve Rotary
explanation: A full organ rotary-speaker chain fed by an overdriven tube preamp. A warm valve stage with grid bias adds second-harmonic warmth that grows into a growl as Drive rises, then feeds a twin-rotor rotating speaker: the signal is split into a bass-rotor and a treble horn band, each spun through its own virtual driver for amplitude tremolo plus a short Doppler pitch vibrato. The horn turns faster than the drum in opposite phase, and Speed morphs slow chorale to fast tremolo with inertia so the rotors ramp rather than jump. Controls: Speed, Drive, Depth, Tone and dry/wet Mix.

name: Cozy Delay
explanation: A warm, dark, short bucket-brigade-style analog delay. A compact interpolated delay line (~20-300 ms) feeds a bounded feedback path; each repeat is made progressively darker and softer by a cascaded low-pass inside the loop plus gentle per-pass saturation, so a string of echoes melts from a present slapback into a soft, intimate shadow. A faint wow drift adds vintage warmth. Controls: Time, Feedback, Tone and dry/wet Mix.

name: Warm Flanger
explanation: A lush, warm analog-voiced flanger in the bucket-brigade tradition. A short fractional delay line is swept by a slow triangle LFO around a parked centre set by Manual; Width sets how far the comb sweeps, Rate the speed, and Regen the feedback. The feedback path is gently low-passed and softly saturated so heavy Regen thickens and resonates creamily instead of turning clangy. A small stereo LFO offset gives a gentle moving image. Controls: Manual, Width, Rate, Regen and dry/wet Mix.

name: Quad Dimension
explanation: A clean, hi-fi dimensional stereo chorus with four fixed mode buttons instead of rate and depth knobs. Each mode (1 = subtle to 4 = widest) preselects a dimensional size that builds an anti-phase side signal from a pair of short, gently de-tuned delay taps per channel, widening and thickening the stereo image with almost no audible pitch wobble. The modulation is kept very slow and shallow so it shimmers rather than warbles; the mono sum stays stable. Controls: Mode (1..4), Width (stereo spread), Tone (dark to bright sparkle) and dry/wet Mix.

name: Master Glue
explanation: A classic British console-style mix-bus 'glue' compressor for gelling a whole mix into one cohesive, punchy whole. A feed-forward, stereo-LINKED VCA detector watches the summed program and drives a single soft-knee gain-reduction element computed in the dB domain, so the same reduction hits both channels and the stereo image stays rock-solid. Ratio is stepped between the classic 2:1, 4:1 and 10:1 settings, Attack is stepped, and Release offers four fixed times plus an AUTO position whose program-dependent dual time-constant 'breathes' with the music — fast on transients, slow under sustained loudness. Makeup restores level, Mix blends parallel dry for New-York glue, and a soft output stage keeps the bus bounded. Controls: Threshold, Ratio, Attack, Release, Makeup and Mix.

name: Tower Spring
explanation: An original model of a tall studio spring-reverb tank: a long cascade of dispersive all-pass lines smears transients into a clean, bright 'boing/chirp' that feeds a long, lightly-modulated stereo feedback delay for a smooth, hi-fi tail up to several seconds. Decay lengthens the tail, Tone tilts dark to bright, Boing sets the dispersion/chirp amount, Width spreads the two decorrelated spring loops, and Mix blends dry/wet.

name: Wide Ensemble
explanation: A lush bucket-brigade (BBD) stereo chorus ensemble with a vibrato mode. A mono-summed input is fanned into a wide stereo image by two modulated delay lines whose sweep runs in anti-phase on the left and right, so the channels swirl against each other for a big ensemble. The Mode control morphs from chorus (dry plus modulated taps) to vibrato (pure modulated tap, so the whole signal pitch-wobbles). A BBD-darkness Tone low-passes the wet path and a soft saturation emulates compander grit for warm analog character. Controls: Rate, Depth, Mode, Tone and dry/wet Mix.

name: Amber Crunch
explanation: A compressed germanium hard-clip distortion in the two-knob vintage lineage. A single high-gain stage drives a pair of soft germanium/LED clipping diodes to ground, giving a smooth-yet-fuzzy, round and slightly dark distortion. Distortion sweeps from light grit to a thick compressed wall; a gentle post Tone tilt and an Output level finish it, with a dry/wet Mix. Controls: Distortion, Output, Tone and Mix.

name: Room Print
explanation: A convolution reverb that prints your sound into a real, measured acoustic space. A genuine room impulse response is baked into the plugin and convolved with the input in the time domain, so the reverb is the true fingerprint of a physical room rather than an algorithm. Controls: dry/wet Mix, Size (how much of the tail is used), Pre-Delay, Tone (high-frequency damping of the tail) and stereo Width. Impulse response: Adventure Kid 'AK-SROOMS' small-room IR, licensed CC BY 4.0.

name: Funk Filter
explanation: An envelope-follower auto-wah: a resonant state-variable filter whose cutoff is swept by the input's own dynamics. Play louder and the peak swoops further; a peak-detecting envelope follower with snappy attack and a musical release tail drives the sweep. Direction flips it (up: louder opens the filter; down: louder closes it), Mode picks a low-pass or a vocal band-pass voice, Sensitivity sets how hard the envelope pushes, Resonance sets the Q/peak, and Range sets the span of the sweep. The classic funky, vocal 'wow' that tracks your playing. Controls: Sensitivity, Resonance, Range, Direction, Mode and dry/wet Mix.

name: Hold Echo
explanation: A studio digital delay with modulation and infinite hold. A clean delay line feeds linear-interpolated repeats whose read tap is gently swept by a quadrature LFO for chorus / pitch-wobble echoes; a tilt tone filter darkens or brightens the feedback path, and a Hold control lifts feedback toward unity while fading the input out so the captured buffer loops and freezes without runaway. A soft limiter keeps the loop bounded. Controls: Time, Feedback, Modulation, Tone, Hold and dry/wet Mix.

name: Steel Flanger
explanation: An extreme, metallic jet-engine flanger. A swept short delay with strong regeneration drives the comb filter into clangy, almost-pitched stainless resonance. A triangle LFO sweeps a fractional delay around a Manual base position over a very wide range, while bipolar Feedback intensifies the metallic ring (positive) or hollows it out (negative through-zero hiss). A soft saturator inside the feedback path keeps the resonance bounded but aggressive. Controls: Rate, Depth, Manual, Feedback and dry/wet Mix.

name: Sweet Drive
explanation: A warm asymmetric soft-clip overdrive. The signal is band-limited to clean the low end, then pushed into an asymmetric waveshaper that clips one half harder than the other — generating even harmonics for a sweeter, slightly fatter break-up over a gentle mid-hump. Touch-sensitive, amp-like dynamics; a post tone low-pass shapes brightness, with output Level and dry/wet Mix. Controls: Drive, Tone, Level, Mix.

name: Bender Fuzz
explanation: A thick, gated germanium fuzz in the vintage three-transistor lineage. Three cascaded asymmetric germanium-style clipping stages build a hard, mid-forward wall of fuzz that is grittier and more aggressive than a typical Fuzz Face or Big Muff. An envelope-tracking gate chokes the output as notes decay, giving the ragged staccato cut-off and 'spit' the circuit is famous for. A tilt Tone control shapes brightness and Level sets output. Controls: Fuzz, Gate, Tone, Level.

name: Brit Distortion
explanation: An amp-in-a-box British distortion. A tightening high-pass feeds a hot gain stage into a soft-knee/hard-rail clipper (the diode + op-amp behaviour of a cranked British amp), which then drives an interactive passive 3-band tone stack: a low shelf (Bass), a peaking bell around 650 Hz (Mid) and a high shelf (Treble). The bands load each other like a real passive network, so you can dial scooped 'crunch' or mid-forward 'roar'. Controls: Gain, Bass, Mid, Treble and Level.

name: Tube Echo
explanation: A single-head tape echo with tube-preamp warmth. One record/play tape head provides a single delayed repeat fed back on itself; a tube preamp stage adds the signature warm saturation that colours the signal even at 100% dry. Each repeat is gently darkened by tape HF loss, softly saturated, and pitch-wandered by slow wow and faster flutter. Feedback can build toward bounded self-oscillation. Controls: Time, Feedback, Drive (preamp warmth), Tone (repeat darkening) and dry/wet Mix.

name: Gush Phaser
explanation: A 4-stage OTA phaser with a gushy, watery, deep sweep. Four cascaded allpass filters are swept by a triangle LFO so the notches glide up and down the spectrum (Rate sets the speed, Depth the span). A Color control feeds part of the chain output back into its input, adding bounded resonant feedback that sharpens the sweep into a vocal, gushing whoosh. Controls: Rate, Depth, Color and dry/wet Mix.

name: Drip Tank
explanation: A drippy outboard spring-reverb tank — the long, boingy surf-amp spring sound, not a tight studio plate. Three parallel spring lines, each a chain of dispersive allpass filters (high frequencies arrive before low ones, giving the signature chirpy 'drip' and flutter) feeding a short damped delay loop. A built-in transient detector fires an excitation burst into the tank, so hard hits audibly boing. Controls: Mix, Dwell (send/level into the tank), Boing (excitation/drip intensity), Tone (dark to bright) and Decay (tail length). Bounded feedback — it never runs away.

name: Opto Trem
explanation: An optical stereo tremolo: a low-frequency oscillator drives a smoothed photocell-style gain cell, modelling the gentle lag of a light-dependent resistor so even hard shapes pulse musically. Shape selects the LFO contour (sine, triangle, square or ramp), Rate and Depth set the throb, and Stereo morphs from a mono tremolo to an auto-pan where the L/R cells run in anti-phase to sweep the image side to side. Clean amplitude modulation with no distortion. Controls: Rate, Depth, Shape, Stereo and Mix.

name: Micro Shift
explanation: A micro-pitch detune doubler that fattens and widens a source into a lush stereo double. Two pitch-shifted voices are detuned a few cents up and down (below a semitone), each given its own short delay tap, panned hard left/right and blended with the dry signal. Fractional delay-line pitch shifting keeps it smooth with no zipper noise. Controls: Detune (cent spread), Delay (tap time), Width (stereo spread), Feedback (subtle regen) and dry/wet Mix.

name: Air Lift
explanation: An air-band shelving EQ: the silky high-shelf specialist. A gentle, wide AIR high shelf opens and brightens the very top without harshness, with a selectable corner that climbs up into the highs (2.5k / 5k / 10k / 20k / 40k). Beneath it sit a musical LOW shelf and a broad MID bell, plus an OUTPUT trim. All bands are clean, stable biquads — boost-only air with a soft slope so the top lifts instead of spiking. Controls: Air, Air Freq, Low, Mid and Output.

name: Mu Leveler
explanation: A vari-mu tube-style compressor and leveler. It models a variable-mu valve gain stage, where the tube's effective gain falls as the signal gets louder, so compression is soft, rounded and program-dependent rather than the hard, fixed-ratio grab of a VCA or FET. Detection runs in the dB domain with a wide, soft knee; the recovery 'breathes', speeding up under dense program material and relaxing as the music opens out. A touch of warm, mostly even-harmonic valve saturation is added on the way out, growing with the Input drive. Controls: Input, Threshold, Recovery, Makeup and dry/wet Mix.

name: Vowel Box
explanation: A talk-box-style formant filter that makes your input sing vowels. Three resonant band-pass formant filters track the F1/F2/F3 peaks of the vowels A-E-I-O-U; sweep the Vowel control and the peaks morph smoothly between vowel shapes. Drive adds harmonics for the formants to bite into, Resonance sharpens the peaks, and Mix blends against the dry signal. Best on rich, harmonic sources.

name: Lattice Verb
explanation: A classic algorithmic reverb built from the textbook Schroeder/Moorer topology: four parallel feedback comb filters with prime delay lengths are summed, each with a one-pole high-frequency damper in its feedback path, then passed through two series allpass diffusers that smear the echoes into a smooth, controllable tail. Controls: Mix, Size (scales the comb delay lengths), Decay (comb feedback / RT60), Damping (HF loss per pass) and Pre-Delay.

name: Diode Comp
explanation: A diode-bridge style bus compressor with a smooth, slightly coloured character. A stereo-linked peak/RMS detector feeds a dB-domain gain computer with a wide over-easy soft knee; Attack and Release shape the gain-reduction envelope. The signal passes through a gentle asymmetric diode-bridge transfer that adds a touch of even-harmonic warmth, so loud material is squeezed and coloured more than quiet passages for a classy, glued sound. Controls: Threshold, Ratio, Attack, Release and Makeup.

name: Iron Drive
explanation: Transformer-style iron-core saturation. The iron saturates earliest in the lows, so a tunable low-end push is fed back into the drive stage, a hysteresis-flavoured soft saturator adds asymmetric even + odd harmonic warmth, and a gentle high-frequency rounding tames the top. A post Tone tilt, dry/wet Mix and Output trim finish it. Controls: Drive, Low, Tone, Mix and Output.

name: Discrete EQ
explanation: A punchy, forward discrete-electronics console equaliser. Three cascaded bands modelled on a vintage 500-series discrete-op-amp EQ: a low band that switches between musical shelf and bell, a sweepable mid bell with reciprocal proportional-Q (the bell sits wide at small boosts and narrows as you push it hard), and a high band that switches between shelf and bell. The whole strip is followed by a touch of discrete-stage drive for that forward console weight. Controls: Low Gain, Low Shape (shelf/bell), Mid Freq, Mid Gain, High Gain, High Shape (shelf/bell) and Drive.

name: Sonic Max
explanation: A psychoacoustic clarity and phase enhancer. The signal is split into low, mid and high bands; the lows are delayed a touch to re-align their timing against the highs, restoring transient punch. Process lifts high-frequency presence for air and definition, while Lo Contour blooms the low end for weight and body. The bands recombine through a soft output trim and dry/wet Mix, so the effect stays subtle and bounded. Controls: Process, Lo Contour, Output and Mix.

name: Whammy
explanation: An extreme expression-pedal pitch shifter. A dual-pointer, crossfaded delay-line shifter chases a target pitch ratio that the Pedal sweeps from dry (heel) to full shift (toe), so you can dive-bomb and soar in real time. Mode selects the direction — 0 up, 1 down, 2 a shimmering dual-octave stack — across a wide ±24-semitone Pitch range. Crossfaded read pointers keep big pitch leaps and dives click-free. Controls: Pitch, Pedal, Mode and dry/wet Mix.

name: Squelch Filter
explanation: An acid envelope filter: a resonant 4-pole transistor-ladder low-pass whose cutoff is opened by an envelope follower tracking the input dynamics, summed with a manual base cutoff. High resonance gives the signature squelch and can near self-oscillation while a saturated feedback path keeps it stable. On transients the filter snaps open and quacks shut. Controls: Cutoff, Resonance, Env Amount, Decay and dry/wet Mix.

name: Freq Shifter
explanation: A Bode-style single-sideband frequency shifter. It splits the input into a 90-degree quadrature pair with a Hilbert-transform allpass network, modulates by a quadrature carrier, and keeps only one sideband — shifting every frequency by a fixed number of Hertz rather than by a ratio. A harmonic input becomes inharmonic and metallic. Controls: Shift (-500..500 Hz), Sideband (down/up), Feedback for shimmering inharmonic cascades, and dry/wet Mix.

name: Scream Filter
explanation: An aggressive Sallen-Key resonant filter. A high-pass and a low-pass run in series, each a 2-pole cell with a saturated resonance feedback path that can ring up to self-oscillation and scream. Signal is driven into that feedback with a tanh nonlinearity for the characteristic biting, distorted tone; the saturator also caps the self-oscillation so the output stays stable at extreme settings. Controls: LP Cutoff, HP Cutoff, Resonance, Drive and dry/wet Mix.

name: Pitch Shifter
explanation: A delay-line pitch shifter and harmonizer. A circular delay line is read by two crossfaded pointers that drift at a rate set by the pitch ratio, producing a click-free shifted voice that is regenerated through a feedback path and blended with the dry signal. Controls: Shift (semitones), Fine (cents), Feedback and dry/wet Mix.

name: Granular Cloud
explanation: A granular delay / cloud processor. Incoming audio is captured into a ring buffer and resprayed as a swarm of overlapping Hann-windowed grains, each read from a delayed, spray-randomised position at a chosen pitch. Controls: Size, Density, Pitch, Spray, Feedback and Mix.

name: Air Exciter
explanation: A psychoacoustic harmonic exciter that adds air and presence. It splits off the upper band, runs it through an asymmetric soft-saturator to synthesise new high-frequency harmonics that were not in the dry signal, brightens that stream with an Air tilt, and blends a controlled amount back on top of the untouched dry path. Controls: Tune, Amount, Air and Mix.

name: Wave Folder
explanation: A west-coast style wavefolder: it drives the signal hard so its peaks fold back on themselves through reflective triangle and sine folds, spawning dense, metallic harmonics instead of flat clipping. Fold sets how many times the wave folds, Symmetry biases the fold axis for even harmonics, and Tone, Output and Mix shape the result.
